newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh cyclone victims face chaos in aftermath.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh cyclone victims face chaos in aftermath.

text.p: Survivors of Monday's cyclone that killed hundreds of people and left thousands missing in Bangladesh said on Tuesday they desperately needed immediate help to rebuild their homes.
"Piecing together the battered lives is the most immediate priority but rebuilding the homes has to come first," said M.A. Mannan, Principal of a college in Kutubdia island in the Bay of Bengal.

"It's almost a race against the time. The monsoon is approaching and thousands of families cannot be left under the sky," he told reporters accompanying Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on a whirlwind tour of the devastated areas.
Hasina promised immediate assistance for the cyclone victims, saying "you are not alone in this hour of need."
The confirmed death toll from Monday's killer cyclone rose to 108 on Tuesday night, with officials saying the number will rise.
They said at least 400,000 houses had been blown down by the 200 kph (125 mph) cyclone, making at least one million people homeless.
Bangladesh's worst cyclone that killed 138,000 people in 1991 had swept the Kutubdia island, 40 km (25 miles) from Cox's Bazar resort town, virtually clean.
Reporters flying with the prime minister in an airforce helicopter on Tuesday saw villages levelled to the ground and people scrambling for relief goods.
Many areas were flooded after embankments were breached, leaving people marooned.
"Shelter is our main concern at the moment, not food or medicine," said Kutubdia resident Mohammad Ullah. The salt farm he worked for has been washed away and his thatched house demolished.
Kutubdia officials said 80 percent of houses on this fishing island were completely or partially damaged.
Power and telecommunications networks in the affected areas collapsed, seriously affecting relief and rehabilitation work.
Hasina on Tuesday had some relief materials distributed and asked government officials to ensure further assistance.
"Home is what they need first. We have to help them with building materials," she told officials at Cox's Bazar and Chittagong.
Hasina sent at least four ministers to different islands to supervise relief operation and rehabilitation.
The Prime Minister, who cancelled a trip to Spain on Sunday in the wake of the cyclone, plans to tour more remote islands on Wednesday, her aides said.
Rescue officials said more than 1,500 fishermen were still missing after the cyclone. "Many of the missing may not return eventually," one official said.
The Fishing Trawler Association in Cox's Bazar echoed the officials fears.
Officials in Maheshkhali island, six km (four miles) from Cox's Bazar, said 500 fishing boats were missing.
They went to the sea or could not rush back to shore despite frequent warnings broadcast over radio, they said.
Hasina expressed her satisfaction over the rescue and relief efforts. "I am very much happy at the way the massive disaster is being tackled," she said.
Islanders and weathermen said casualties had been lower because the cyclone struck during the day and at low tide.
High waves triggered by strong winds washed over some 15,000 shrimp farms, causing heavy losses, officials said.
